extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and other patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying and handling judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) in patent claims, with illustrative examples and a case-law chart summarizing eligibility findings. Intended to help examiners determine when a detailed subject-matter eligibility analysis is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of a judicial exception triggers further analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of a judicial exception in a claim merely indicates further analysis for eligibility should be conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim recites a concept that falls within a judicial exception, examiners must perform the eligibility analysis (e.g., the Alice/Mayo two-step). Identifying an exception is not itself a final determination of ineligibility; it signals the need for additional inquiry into whether the claim as a whole is directed to, or amounts to, practical application or significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: No bright lines between exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: As explained in the guidance, there are no bright lines between exceptions as many can be characterized under several types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect strict categorical boundaries: a concept may be described as a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, and/or an abstract idea depending on characterization. Examiners should consider multiple characterizations and apply the eligibility framework flexibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists are illustrative and not limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: These lists are intended to be illustrative and not limiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The enumerated examples of judicial exceptions (and case examples) are examples only; absence from the list does not mean a concept cannot be a judicial exception. Examiners must evaluate claims on their own merits and may encounter other concepts that qualify as exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of laws of nature and natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of laws of nature and natural phenomena: An isolated DNA; A correlation that is the consequence of how a certain compound is metabolized by the body; Electromagnetism to transmit signals; The chemical principle underlying the union between fatty elements and water; The Arrhenius equation for calculating the cure time of rubber; (and similar natural laws/phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete examples (drawn from court decisions) illustrate the types of concepts courts have treated as laws of nature or natural phenomena. Use them to inform, but not constrain, claim analysis. Where claims recite such concepts, determine whether the claim integrates the concept into a practical application or is merely directed to the concept itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of abstract ideas: Mitigating settlement risk; Hedging; Creating a contractual relationship; Using advertising as an exchange or currency; Processing information through a clearinghouse; Generating insurance-policy-related tasks based on rules to be completed upon the occurrence of an event; Managing a stable-value protected life insurance policy; Comparing new and stored information and using rules to identify options; Comparing a patient’s gene with the wild-type gene, and identifying any differences that arise; Collecting data, recognizing certain data within the collected data set, and storing that recognized data in a memory; Using categories to organize, store, and transmit information; Organizing information through mathematical correlations; Managing a game of Bingo; A formula for updating alarm limits; A mathematical formula relating to standing wave phenomena; A mathematical procedure for converting one form of numerical representation to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are illustrative abstract-idea concepts identified in case law. When claims involve processes such as mental steps, fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, or mathematical relationships, examiners should evaluate whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea and, if so, whether additional claim elements transform it into a patent-eligible application (i.e., provide 'significantly more').

rubrics_metrics.name: Case chart content and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For each case (arranged in chronological order), the chart provides: (1) a link to the entire court opinion, (2) the patent number(s) or application number(s) at issue, (3) the subject matter of the patent/application, (4) whether the claims were eligible or ineligible, and (5) the USPC/CPC classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chart is a factual reference tool for examiners. Each entry gives the citation and factual context needed to compare a pending application to precedent. The chart will be updated with future decisions; use the links to read full opinions for detailed reasoning rather than relying solely on the chart summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the case chart to identify applications needing detailed eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may find this information useful in identifying those applications that may require a detailed eligibility analysis during examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similarities in subject matter, claim scope, and classification as prompts to examine eligibility more carefully, but do not treat chart similarity as dispositive. Follow the prescribed eligibility analysis and consult the cited opinions for reasoning and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each case turns on its own facts — similarity is not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to remember that each case turns on its own facts. Therefore, the mere fact that a pending application may be similarly classified to a patent or an application in this chart, or have similar subject matter, does not necessarily indicate an eligibility issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing a pending application to cases in the chart, focus on the actual claim language, asserted inventive concept, and factual detail in the court's analysis. Do not infer eligibility outcomes solely from classification or high-level topic similarity; perform the full legal and factual analysis.
